courses.description: A separate book-based course: 31 chapters, 170 section lessons, a searchable glossary, and an editorial 6th Edition crosswalk.
courses.provenance: Derived from your uploaded Applied Behavior Analysis, Third Edition, by John O. Cooper, Timothy E. Heron, and William L. Heward (Pearson; copyright page 2020). Chapter lessons paraphrase the book; glossary and source-reader text are extracted from the supplied copy. The 170 application scenarios are newly written study exercises, not textbook cases, official exam items, or a validated question bank. The book’s printed task mappings reference the 5th Edition. This app’s 6th Edition crosswalk is separate editorial work and marks limited/unmapped coverage. It is not endorsed by Pearson, the authors, or the BACB. No independent clinical or exam-completeness review has been performed.

topics.title: Science: Basic Characteristics and a Definition
topics.summary: The chapter treats science as a systematic way to understand natural events. Description, prediction, and control are different products of inquiry; the attitudes of science guide how claims are examined.

concepts.definition: Systematically observe, quantify, and classify events. Descriptive results can suggest questions but do not establish that one event caused another.
Repeated covariation permits a probabilistic forecast. A correlation does not, by itself, identify a causal relation.
Systematic manipulation of an independent variable reliably changes a dependent variable, with competing explanations sufficiently controlled.

Determinism assumes lawful relations; empiricism requires observation; experimentation tests relations; replication checks reliability; parsimony rules out simpler explanations; philosophic doubt keeps conclusions open to revision.

topics.takeaway: A plausible explanation and a strong correlation are not substitutes for experimental evidence.

scenario.prompt: A teacher records that interruptions are more frequent on days with substitute staff. Nothing is experimentally changed. What level of understanding does the repeated association support?
options: Prediction
Proof of a staffing function
Experimental control
Replication of an intervention
scenario.explanation: The repeated association can support a forecast, but substitute staffing has not been isolated as a cause.
rationales: The repeated association can support a forecast, but substitute staffing has not been isolated as a cause.
The description does not isolate staffing from other changes on those days.
Control requires systematic manipulation and a convincing functional relation, not covariation alone.
No intervention has been introduced and replicated.

topics.title: A Brief History of Behavior Analysis
topics.summary: The authors locate applied behavior analysis within its philosophical and experimental history. Their account distinguishes Watson’s stimulus-response program, Skinner’s experimental analysis, radical behaviorism, and the emergence of applied research.

concepts.definition: The philosophical branch asks what a science of behavior studies, how knowledge is obtained, and how behavior is explained.
The basic-research branch investigates orderly behavior–environment relations using controlled experiments and repeated measurement.
Private events such as thinking and feeling are included in a natural-science account. Limited public accessibility does not place them in a separate causal world.
Renaming behavior with an inferred inner entity can create circular explanation without identifying the variables responsible for the behavior.

topics.takeaway: Including private events is different from explaining behavior by an unexplained inner agent.

scenario.prompt: An explanation states, “Mira avoids assignments because she has avoidance tendencies,” and offers no independent evidence. Which concern from the chapter applies?
options: An unconditioned reflex
Explanatory fiction
Exclusion of all private behavior
A demonstrated functional relation
scenario.explanation: The explanation redescribes the observed avoidance rather than identifying controlling variables.
rationales: No eliciting stimulus–reflex relation has been specified.
The explanation redescribes the observed avoidance rather than identifying controlling variables.
The problem is circular explanation, not the mere inclusion of private events.
No variable was manipulated to demonstrate a relation.

topics.title: Characteristics of Applied Behavior Analysis
topics.summary: The seven dimensions are criteria for judging behavior-analytic work, not seven treatment techniques. They concern the importance of the target, measurement, causal analysis, procedural description, conceptual grounding, practical impact, and generality.

concepts.definition: Choose behavior of social importance and measure the actual behavior in need of improvement. Check whose behavior changed, including possible observer changes.
Demonstrate a believable functional relation between manipulated events and changes in the measured behavior.
Describe procedures sufficiently for replication and connect them to behavioral principles rather than presenting disconnected tricks.
Produce a practically important improvement that endures, occurs in relevant other settings, or extends to other useful behaviors.

topics.takeaway: A program can improve a measured behavior yet still fail to produce a meaningful benefit in the person’s life.

scenario.prompt: A report says “staff used appropriate reinforcement,” but never defines what staff did or when they did it. Which dimension is most directly compromised?
options: Generality
Behavioral
Technological
Applied
scenario.explanation: Another trained person could not reliably reproduce the procedure from that description.
rationales: The omission concerns procedural reproducibility, not transfer across settings or time.
The scenario does not identify a failure to measure the target behavior.
Another trained person could not reliably reproduce the procedure from that description.
The social importance of the target is not specified as the problem.

cards.answer: Choose behavior of social importance and measure the actual behavior in need of improvement. Check whose behavior changed, including possible observer changes.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Effective and generality?

topics.title: A Definition of Applied Behavior Analysis
topics.summary: The book defines ABA through two linked purposes: improving socially significant behavior and identifying the variables responsible for that improvement. It also distinguishes research from professional services informed by research.

concepts.definition: Behavior-change tactics are derived from behavioral principles, applied systematically, and evaluated experimentally to identify responsible variables.
Radical behaviorism addresses philosophy; EAB addresses basic research; ABA addresses applied research; professional practice delivers services guided by that science.
Basic and applied research inform each other. Translation is not limited to a one-way movement from a laboratory to practice.

topics.takeaway: Providing evidence-informed services and conducting applied experimental research are related activities, not identical labels.

scenario.prompt: A practitioner uses established procedures to help one client communicate, but is not conducting an experiment intended to contribute new research findings. Which domain best describes the primary activity?
options: Translational research by definition
Radical behaviorism alone
Experimental analysis of behavior
Professional practice guided by behavior analysis
scenario.explanation: The activity is individualized service delivery informed by the science.
rationales: Using research in practice does not automatically constitute a new research project.
The primary activity is service delivery, not philosophical analysis.
This is not a basic laboratory investigation.
The activity is individualized service delivery informed by the science.

topics.title: Behavior
topics.summary: Behavior is treated as an organism’s interaction with its environment, not a possession or static trait. A response is an instance; a response class groups responses by a common environmental effect.

concepts.definition: Behavior refers to activity or a class of activity. A response is a particular instance of that activity.
The physical form of a response. Similar forms can have different functions, and different forms can have the same function.
A group of responses that produce the same effect on the environment, even when their movements differ.
The behaviors a person can perform, or a collection of skills relevant to a particular task or setting.

topics.takeaway: Classify a response by the relevant relation, not merely by its appearance.

scenario.prompt: A person opens a door by pushing it with a hand, shoulder, or foot. All three actions open the door. What groups these actions functionally?
options: A response class
One identical response topography
A stimulus class
A static personal trait
scenario.explanation: Different topographies share the same environmental effect: opening the door.
rationales: Different topographies share the same environmental effect: opening the door.
The movements differ.
The examples describe actions, not a set of antecedent stimuli.
The examples are interactions with the environment rather than a trait.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Behavior and response?
cards.answer: Behavior refers to activity or a class of activity. A response is a particular instance of that activity.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Response topography?
cards.answer: The physical form of a response. Similar forms can have different functions, and different forms can have the same function.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Response class?
cards.answer: A group of responses that produce the same effect on the environment, even when their movements differ.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Repertoire?
cards.answer: The behaviors a person can perform, or a collection of skills relevant to a particular task or setting.

topics.title: Environment
topics.summary: The relevant environment includes physical conditions both outside and within the body. Stimuli can be described by their physical features, timing relative to behavior, and behavioral functions.

concepts.definition: A stimulus is an energy change affecting an organism through receptor cells. A stimulus class shares specified formal, temporal, or functional properties.
An antecedent exists or occurs before the behavior of interest; a consequence is a stimulus change following it.
Another person may arrange antecedents or consequences. A nonsocial environmental event can also influence behavior.
One event can have more than one behavioral effect. Physical appearance alone does not identify those effects.

topics.takeaway: Before assigning a function, identify the behavior of interest and the event’s temporal relation to it.

scenario.prompt: A timer sounds; Ari turns off the timer; the sound stops. Relative to turning it off, which event is the consequence?
options: The timer starting to sound
The sound stopping
Ari’s hand movement
The timer’s color
scenario.explanation: The termination follows the response; its reinforcing function would require evidence about future responding.
rationales: That event precedes the response.
The termination follows the response; its reinforcing function would require evidence about future responding.
That is the behavior of interest, not its consequence.
A physical feature is not the described postresponse change.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Stimulus and stimulus class?
cards.answer: A stimulus is an energy change affecting an organism through receptor cells. A stimulus class shares specified formal, temporal, or functional properties.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Antecedent and consequence?
cards.answer: An antecedent exists or occurs before the behavior of interest; a consequence is a stimulus change following it.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Social mediation?
cards.answer: Another person may arrange antecedents or consequences. A nonsocial environmental event can also influence behavior.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Multiple stimulus functions?
cards.answer: One event can have more than one behavioral effect. Physical appearance alone does not identify those effects.

topics.title: Respondent Behavior
topics.summary: Respondent behavior is elicited by antecedent stimuli. Respondent conditioning changes which stimuli elicit a response; respondent extinction concerns repeated presentation of the conditioned stimulus without the relevant unconditioned stimulus.

concepts.definition: A stimulus–response relation that does not require the individual’s prior pairing history.
Pairing a neutral stimulus with an eliciting stimulus can establish the formerly neutral event as a conditioned stimulus.
A neutral stimulus can acquire eliciting properties through pairing with an already conditioned stimulus.
Habituation is diminished responding with repeated eliciting stimulation; respondent extinction follows CS presentations without the US.

topics.takeaway: Distinguish a stimulus–stimulus pairing procedure from a response–consequence contingency.

scenario.prompt: After a sound has been repeatedly paired with an air puff, the sound alone elicits blinking. Later the sound is repeatedly presented without the puff and blinking weakens. What is the latter procedure?
options: Shaping
Operant extinction
Respondent extinction
Negative punishment
scenario.explanation: The conditioned stimulus occurs without the unconditioned stimulus.
rationales: No successive response approximations are being differentially reinforced.
The example concerns elicitation and stimulus pairing, not withholding a consequence for an operant.
The conditioned stimulus occurs without the unconditioned stimulus.
No response-contingent loss of a reinforcer is described.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Unconditioned reflex?
cards.answer: A stimulus–response relation that does not require the individual’s prior pairing history.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Respondent conditioning?
cards.answer: Pairing a neutral stimulus with an eliciting stimulus can establish the formerly neutral event as a conditioned stimulus.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Higher-order conditioning?
cards.answer: A neutral stimulus can acquire eliciting properties through pairing with an already conditioned stimulus.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Habituation versus respondent extinction?
cards.answer: Habituation is diminished responding with repeated eliciting stimulation; respondent extinction follows CS presentations without the US.

topics.title: Operant Behavior
topics.summary: Operant behavior is selected by its consequences. Consequences affect future members of a response class, and their behavioral functions must be demonstrated rather than inferred from good intentions or stimulus labels.

concepts.definition: Reinforcement increases future responding; punishment decreases it. Positive and negative refer to stimulus presentation and withdrawal, not moral value.
Automaticity means that awareness is not required. Automatic reinforcement means the consequence is not socially mediated.
Ontogenic selection operates during an individual’s life. The chapter relates this to phylogenic selection and social-cultural contingencies.
A response class occurs differentially in antecedent conditions associated with different consequences. The three-term contingency comprises antecedent, behavior, and consequence.
Some stimuli function without prior pairing; others acquire reinforcing or punishing functions through learning history. Current conditions remain important.

topics.takeaway: The same stimulus can have different functions for different behaviors, people, and conditions.

scenario.prompt: A supervisor adds public praise after reports are submitted. Submission becomes less frequent. Under the described conditions, what function has the added praise had?
options: Positive reinforcement
No possible behavioral function because praise is pleasant
Negative reinforcement
Positive punishment
scenario.explanation: An added consequence is followed by a decrease in the future behavior, regardless of the supervisor’s intention.
rationales: Reinforcement would require increased future submission.
A stimulus is not assigned a fixed function by its ordinary label.
No stimulus withdrawal and increase in responding are described.
An added consequence is followed by a decrease in the future behavior, regardless of the supervisor’s intention.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Reinforcement and punishment?
cards.answer: Reinforcement increases future responding; punishment decreases it. Positive and negative refer to stimulus presentation and withdrawal, not moral value.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Automaticity versus automatic reinforcement?
cards.answer: Automaticity means that awareness is not required. Automatic reinforcement means the consequence is not socially mediated.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Selection by consequences?
cards.answer: Ontogenic selection operates during an individual’s life. The chapter relates this to phylogenic selection and social-cultural contingencies.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Discriminated operant?
cards.answer: A response class occurs differentially in antecedent conditions associated with different consequences. The three-term contingency comprises antecedent, behavior, and consequence.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Unconditioned and conditioned consequences?
cards.answer: Some stimuli function without prior pairing; others acquire reinforcing or punishing functions through learning history. Current conditions remain important.

topics.title: Recognizing the Complexity of Human Behavior
topics.summary: Human behavior is multiply determined and often includes verbal rules, response chains, and emergent performances. The authors emphasize that applied environments and individual learning histories complicate prediction and intervention.

concepts.definition: Behavior under control of a verbal statement specifying a contingency, as distinguished from learning through direct contact with that contingency.
Behavior acquired through direct experience with consequences.
Several variables can influence one response. Joint control involves the converging control of separately established responses with a common topography.
Different histories and physical capacities matter. Logistical, resource, legal, and ethical constraints can limit an applied analysis.

topics.takeaway: An initial success does not establish that all relevant variables or all future conditions are understood.

scenario.prompt: Lee operates unfamiliar equipment correctly after reading its instructions, without previously trying it. Which distinction best describes the initial performance?
options: Rule-governed rather than directly contingency-shaped performance
Respondent rather than operant behavior
Proof that instructions always override contingencies
Behavior without environmental control
scenario.explanation: A verbal description is guiding the response before direct experience with the equipment’s contingencies.
rationales: A verbal description is guiding the response before direct experience with the equipment’s contingencies.
Following instructions is not described as an elicited reflex.
The example establishes no such universal effect.
The written instructions are environmental events with a relevant learning history.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Rule-governed behavior?
cards.answer: Behavior under control of a verbal statement specifying a contingency, as distinguished from learning through direct contact with that contingency.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Contingency-shaped behavior?
cards.answer: Behavior acquired through direct experience with consequences.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Multiple control and joint control?
cards.answer: Several variables can influence one response. Joint control involves the converging control of separately established responses with a common topography.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Individual history and practical constraints?
cards.answer: Different histories and physical capacities matter. Logistical, resource, legal, and ethical constraints can limit an applied analysis.

topics.title: Role of Assessment in Applied Behavior Analysis
topics.summary: Assessment informs planning, implementation, monitoring, and follow-up. Before selecting a target, the analyst must establish authority, permission, relevant skills and resources, and review existing records.

concepts.definition: Indirect, direct, and empirical procedures identify and define behavior and relevant environmental variables.
Screening; defining and quantifying concerns and outcome criteria; pinpointing targets; monitoring progress; following up.
Check permission and professional capability, examine medical and educational information, and consider prior interventions and their implementation.

topics.takeaway: Having a behavioral interpretation does not automatically authorize an assessment or intervention.

scenario.prompt: An analyst observes a stranger’s child in a store and begins offering a treatment plan without a request or service agreement. Which preliminary issue was bypassed?
options: Selecting a reversal design
Authority and permission to assess and intervene
Calculating total-count agreement
Choosing a variable-ratio schedule
scenario.explanation: The chapter distinguishes professional skill from permission to provide services in a particular relationship.
rationales: Experimental design is not the initial missing prerequisite.
The chapter distinguishes professional skill from permission to provide services in a particular relationship.
Measurement agreement cannot create permission.
Schedule selection comes later and does not resolve authority.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Behavioral assessment?
cards.answer: Indirect, direct, and empirical procedures identify and define behavior and relevant environmental variables.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Assessment phases?
cards.answer: Screening; defining and quantifying concerns and outcome criteria; pinpointing targets; monitoring progress; following up.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Preassessment considerations?
cards.answer: Check permission and professional capability, examine medical and educational information, and consider prior interventions and their implementation.

topics.title: Assessment Methods Used by Behavior Analysts
topics.summary: Assessment methods differ in what they observe and what conclusions they support. Interviews can identify concerns and hypotheses; direct observation examines events as they occur; empirical procedures can test relevant relations.

concepts.definition: Interviews, checklists, and rating scales depend on reports, recollections, or judgments. What, when, and where questions help specify events.
Observe the relevant performance or assess specific skills rather than assuming a broad score supplies a treatment target.
Record a temporally ordered account of antecedents, behavior, and consequences in the natural environment.
The assessment process itself can change what is measured. Repeated, unobtrusive observations and cautious interpretation are important.

topics.takeaway: A report about behavior and direct observation of that behavior are different sources of information.

scenario.prompt: A caregiver rates yesterday’s behavior on a questionnaire. Another observer watches today’s routine and records events. How should the first method be classified?
options: Permanent-product measurement
Direct continuous observation
Indirect assessment
Functional analysis
scenario.explanation: The questionnaire relies on a report rather than direct measurement of the events as they occur.
rationales: The score is a report, not a product uniquely generated by the target response.
The caregiver is recalling events rather than recording the described live observation.
The questionnaire relies on a report rather than direct measurement of the events as they occur.
No environmental variable is experimentally manipulated.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Indirect assessment?
cards.answer: Interviews, checklists, and rating scales depend on reports, recollections, or judgments. What, when, and where questions help specify events.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Direct and curriculum-based assessment?
cards.answer: Observe the relevant performance or assess specific skills rather than assuming a broad score supplies a treatment target.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by ABC recording?
cards.answer: Record a temporally ordered account of antecedents, behavior, and consequences in the natural environment.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Reactivity?
cards.answer: The assessment process itself can change what is measured. Repeated, unobtrusive observations and cautious interpretation are important.

topics.title: Assessing the Social Significance of Potential Target Behaviors
topics.summary: The applied target should improve adjustment, competence, and quality of life. The chapter offers questions about natural reinforcement, access to new environments, prerequisites, age appropriateness, and replacement behavior.

concepts.definition: Improvement in the person’s adaptation, competence, and quality of life, rather than change for its own sake.
A useful target should contact reinforcement in the person’s postintervention environment.
A cusp opens access to new environments, contingencies, or reinforcers; a pivotal behavior produces changes in other untrained behaviors.
When reducing behavior, identify a desirable adaptive alternative rather than merely an absence of responding.

topics.takeaway: Ask what the skill makes possible in the learner’s life, not only whether it is easy to teach.

scenario.prompt: Learning to use a bus route gives a learner access to a workplace, recreation center, and new social opportunities. Which concept is especially illustrated?
options: Observer drift
A punishment contingency
A purely topographic improvement
Behavioral cusp
scenario.explanation: The new skill opens contact with additional environments and contingencies beyond the trained response.
rationales: This is a change in the learner’s access, not in measurement criteria.
No response-decreasing consequence is described.
The importance described is its broader functional consequence, not its form alone.
The new skill opens contact with additional environments and contingencies beyond the trained response.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Habilitation?
cards.answer: Improvement in the person’s adaptation, competence, and quality of life, rather than change for its own sake.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Relevance of behavior rule?
cards.answer: A useful target should contact reinforcement in the person’s postintervention environment.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Behavioral cusp versus pivotal behavior?
cards.answer: A cusp opens access to new environments, contingencies, or reinforcers; a pivotal behavior produces changes in other untrained behaviors.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Replacement behavior?
cards.answer: When reducing behavior, identify a desirable adaptive alternative rather than merely an absence of responding.

topics.title: Prioritizing Target Behaviors
topics.summary: Assessment can identify more potential targets than can be addressed at once. Prioritization considers urgency, likely benefit, opportunity for reinforcement, feasibility, and the perspectives of the person and significant others.

concepts.definition: Consider danger, frequency, duration of the problem, access to reinforcement, future independence, likelihood of success, and cost.
The person receiving services and relevant family, staff, and administrators contribute to identifying and prioritizing targets.
Explicit discussion of priorities can expose disagreements before an intervention is launched.

topics.takeaway: Target selection is a reasoned, participatory process rather than a list ordered by convenience.

scenario.prompt: A team chooses handwriting neatness because it is easiest to count, while ignoring frequent unsafe street crossing. What was neglected in prioritization?
options: Relative danger and socially important benefit
The assumption that all stakeholder preferences are identical
A requirement to use punishment first
The need to target only one topography forever
scenario.explanation: Measurement convenience should not displace urgent safety and habilitative considerations.
rationales: Measurement convenience should not displace urgent safety and habilitative considerations.
The chapter recommends participation because priorities can differ.
No such requirement follows from prioritizing safety.
Prioritization does not impose a permanent single-target rule.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Priority dimensions?
cards.answer: Consider danger, frequency, duration of the problem, access to reinforcement, future independence, likelihood of success, and cost.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Stakeholder participation?
cards.answer: The person receiving services and relevant family, staff, and administrators contribute to identifying and prioritizing targets.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Goal conflicts?
cards.answer: Explicit discussion of priorities can expose disagreements before an intervention is launched.

topics.title: Defining Target Behaviors
topics.summary: A usable definition identifies exactly which responses count and which do not. Function-based definitions use a common effect; topography-based definitions use form. Both need sufficient clarity for consistent use.

concepts.definition: Groups responses by their common effect on the environment.
Specifies the form or shape of the behavior, including appropriate inclusion and exclusion rules.
The definition should be objective, clear, and complete. Observers need to distinguish instances from noninstances.
The defined class must capture the actual concern rather than a broader or narrower substitute.

topics.takeaway: “Uncooperative” is a judgment; a measurement definition specifies observable events.

scenario.prompt: Two observers disagree because “disruptive behavior” includes talking for one and only shouting for the other. What should happen first?
options: Select a stronger reinforcer
Clarify the target definition with explicit instances and noninstances
Assume one observer is biased
Average their counts and keep the label
scenario.explanation: A shared objective, clear, complete definition is necessary before agreement data can be interpreted meaningfully.
rationales: Reinforcer selection does not repair an ambiguous measure.
A shared objective, clear, complete definition is necessary before agreement data can be interpreted meaningfully.
The scenario identifies definitional ambiguity, not evidence of deliberate bias.
Averaging does not resolve different response classes.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Function-based definition?
cards.answer: Groups responses by their common effect on the environment.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Topography-based definition?
cards.answer: Specifies the form or shape of the behavior, including appropriate inclusion and exclusion rules.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Definition quality?
cards.answer: The definition should be objective, clear, and complete. Observers need to distinguish instances from noninstances.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Definition validity?
cards.answer: The defined class must capture the actual concern rather than a broader or narrower substitute.

topics.title: Setting Criteria for Behavior Change
topics.summary: Criteria for success should be determined before intervention. The desired magnitude of change is tied to meaningful outcomes, not to an arbitrary percentage selected after viewing the results.

concepts.definition: A specified level of performance that defines the desired or needed change.
Assess competent performers or experimentally examine which performance level produces an important result.
Identify the behavior, relevant conditions, and measurable performance level rather than an unspecified improvement.

topics.takeaway: Choose criteria that answer whether the change matters, not just whether the graph moves.

scenario.prompt: A team announces success whenever performance rises at all, then picks its criterion after treatment ends. What is the stronger planning approach?
options: Avoid criteria to preserve flexibility
Use the same percentage for every possible skill
Set a socially validated performance criterion before treatment
Use the largest number observed as the goal
scenario.explanation: The chapter recommends specifying the needed outcome in advance and linking it to functional benefit.
rationales: Flexibility in procedures does not remove the need to define a meaningful outcome.
Different goals and environments may require different criteria.
The chapter recommends specifying the needed outcome in advance and linking it to functional benefit.
A post hoc maximum does not establish social validity.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Outcome criterion?
cards.answer: A specified level of performance that defines the desired or needed change.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Social validation of criteria?
cards.answer: Assess competent performers or experimentally examine which performance level produces an important result.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Observable goal?
cards.answer: Identify the behavior, relevant conditions, and measurable performance level rather than an unspecified improvement.

topics.title: Definition and Functions of Measurement in Applied Behavior Analysis
topics.summary: Measurement assigns quantitative labels to observed properties using consistent rules. Repeated measurement supports both evaluation of overall effects and decisions made while intervention is occurring.

concepts.definition: A systematic process for assigning quantitative values to observed dimensions of events.
Frequent measures during intervention inform whether to continue, modify, or stop procedures.
Measures before and after intervention help evaluate the overall outcome.
Data can reveal both unnoticed progress and the continuation of ineffective treatment.

topics.takeaway: Without repeated measurement, impressions may cause an effective treatment to be stopped or an ineffective one to continue.

scenario.prompt: A teacher adjusts instruction each week after inspecting daily performance data. Which measurement use is emphasized?
options: Proof of experimental control
Only a terminal outcome assessment
An indirect personality inference
Formative evaluation
scenario.explanation: Repeated data are guiding changes while instruction is in progress.
rationales: Frequent measurement supports decisions but does not alone demonstrate causation.
The decisions occur throughout intervention, not only at its conclusion.
Actual performance is being measured.
Repeated data are guiding changes while instruction is in progress.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Measurement?
cards.answer: A systematic process for assigning quantitative values to observed dimensions of events.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Formative evaluation?
cards.answer: Frequent measures during intervention inform whether to continue, modify, or stop procedures.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Summative evaluation?
cards.answer: Measures before and after intervention help evaluate the overall outcome.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Accountability?
cards.answer: Data can reveal both unnoticed progress and the continuation of ineffective treatment.

topics.title: Measurable Dimensions of Behavior
topics.summary: Different questions require different behavioral dimensions. The chapter distinguishes repeatability, temporal extent, and temporal locus, along with derived measures and other useful parameters.

concepts.definition: Count is the number of occurrences. Rate = count / observation time, reported per specified unit of time.
Duration runs from response onset to offset; latency runs from a stimulus to response onset; interresponse time runs between successive responses.
Percentage = qualifying responses / opportunities × 100. Trials-to-criterion counts opportunities needed to attain a predefined level.
Celeration is change in rate across time. Topography concerns form; magnitude concerns force or intensity.

topics.takeaway: A count is not a rate unless observation time is included.

scenario.prompt: There are 18 responses during a 30-minute observation. What is the rate per minute?
options: 0.6 responses per minute
1.67 responses per minute
60 percent
18 responses per minute
scenario.explanation: Rate is 18 divided by 30 = 0.6 responses per minute.
rationales: Rate is 18 divided by 30 = 0.6 responses per minute.
That inverts time and count.
No opportunity denominator was provided for a percentage.
Eighteen is the session count, not the per-minute rate.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Count and rate?
cards.answer: Count is the number of occurrences. Rate = count / observation time, reported per specified unit of time.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Duration, latency, and IRT?
cards.answer: Duration runs from response onset to offset; latency runs from a stimulus to response onset; interresponse time runs between successive responses.

cards.answer: Celeration is change in rate across time. Topography concerns form; magnitude concerns force or intensity.

topics.title: Methods for Measuring Behavior
topics.summary: Continuous recording seeks to capture the relevant dimension throughout observation. Discontinuous procedures sample intervals or moments and produce estimates whose interpretation depends on the rule used.

concepts.definition: Detect and record individual occurrences when the response is sufficiently discrete and countable.
Score an interval only when the behavior occurs throughout the entire interval.
Score an interval when the behavior occurs at any point within it; this is not a count of occurrences.
Score whether behavior is occurring at the designated moment. PLACHECK applies a momentary observation to the members of a group.

topics.takeaway: Percentage of intervals and percentage of time are not interchangeable.

options: Event count
Partial-interval recording
Momentary time sampling
Whole-interval recording

topics.summary: A permanent product permits measurement after the behavior has occurred. Its usefulness depends on a defensible relation between the target response and the resulting product.

topics.takeaway: An observable product is not automatically valid evidence of who performed the target behavior.

topics.title: Measurement Tools
topics.summary: The chapter describes low-technology and digital measurement tools. The instrument should support accurate recording of the chosen dimension in the actual setting; sophistication alone does not establish measurement quality.

topics.title: Selecting a Measurement Method
topics.summary: Measurement selection begins with the question being asked, the behavior’s features, and practical observation conditions. A procedure should be sensitive to the dimension and direction of change that matter.

concepts.definition: Measure the property central to the concern, such as elapsed engagement time rather than merely starts.
Consider when and where behavior occurs, whether it can be detected reliably, and staff availability and skill.
Use the most suitable feasible procedure while understanding what information sampling omits.

Only the number of starts
The teacher’s satisfaction rating alone

topics.title: Indicators of Trustworthy Measurement
topics.summary: Trustworthy measurement requires distinctions among validity, accuracy, and reliability. Agreement or consistency is useful evidence, but it is not identical to correspondence with the true event.

concepts.definition: Measure the socially significant behavior, the relevant dimension, and representative conditions and times.
Observed values correspond to the true values of the event.
Repeated measurement of the same event yields the same values.

topics.takeaway: A measure can be consistently wrong; reliability does not guarantee accuracy.

topics.title: Threats to Valid Measurement
topics.summary: A valid measure must represent the target concern. Indirect proxies, irrelevant dimensions, poorly scheduled observations, and measurement artifacts can produce a misleading picture even when recording is consistent.

concepts.definition: A measure of a different behavior requires evidence that it reflects the behavior of interest.

Observations should include conditions and times relevant to the reason for measurement, not only convenient periods.

topics.takeaway: Ask whether the data answer the original concern before interpreting apparent improvement.

A guaranteed lack of observer agreement

topics.summary: Measurement error often involves the observer and the recording system. Training, independent measurement, calibration, and protection against expectations help limit drift and bias.

topics.summary: Accuracy checks compare observations with an independently established true value. Reliability checks involve remeasurement of the same event, often using a natural or contrived permanent record.

topics.title: Using Interobserver Agreement to Assess Behavioral Measurement
topics.summary: Interobserver agreement describes the correspondence of independent observations of the same events using the same system. Different IOA formulas answer different questions and can be differently sensitive to disagreement.

topics.title: Purpose and Benefits of Graphic Displays of Behavioral Data
topics.summary: Graphic displays keep the analyst in direct, ongoing contact with behavioral data. They support responsive decisions and let other readers inspect the evidence rather than depend only on a verbal conclusion.

concepts.definition: Data are products of measurement; graphs display relations among measurements and relevant variables.
Plotting observations as they are obtained can reveal emerging changes or unexpected variation that merit investigation.
A clear graph allows others to evaluate the pattern and its practical importance.

topics.takeaway: Graphing is part of analysis, not merely a final illustration of a predetermined conclusion.

Replacing the client’s goals with statistical significance
Ongoing, responsive decision making
Guaranteeing a causal relation from any graph

topics.summary: The chapter compares graph formats by the information each makes visible. Line graphs preserve successive observations; cumulative records show accumulated responding; other formats answer different display questions.

topics.summary: A graph should represent measurements accurately and show the conditions under which they were obtained. Axis choices, missing observations, labels, and connections between points affect what the reader can infer.

topics.summary: Measurement establishes whether and how behavior changed; experimental analysis investigates the relation responsible. The chapter emphasizes individual behavior, repeated measures, and environmental sources of variation.

topics.summary: Baseline logic uses repeated observations to predict performance without intervention, verify that prediction, and replicate the effect of the independent variable. Baseline is a comparison condition, not necessarily an absence of all teaching.

topics.title: Using Reinforcement Effectively
topics.summary: Effective reinforcement programs consider attainable initial criteria, potency and variety of consequences, prompts, descriptive feedback, and the eventual shift toward naturally occurring reinforcement.

concepts.definition: Make the starting criterion attainable and initially reinforce each occurrence of the target response when appropriate.
Use effective consequences of suitable magnitude and variety while considering motivating operations.
Combine support for correct responding with consequences and feedback tied clearly to the response.
Gradually alter delays and contrived supports as performance permits rather than remove all support abruptly.

topics.takeaway: An acquisition arrangement should also anticipate how useful behavior will be maintained outside training.

scenario.prompt: A new skill is rarely emitted, and the first reinforcement criterion requires twenty perfect consecutive performances. What adjustment is most consistent with this section?
options: Remove all feedback permanently
Make the criterion even harder immediately
Assume the selected consequence is ineffective without testing
Begin with an attainable criterion that allows contact with reinforcement
scenario.explanation: An initially unreachable requirement provides little opportunity to strengthen the emerging response.
rationales: The chapter describes useful roles for feedback and descriptive praise.
That further reduces the opportunity to contact the consequence.
Lack of responding under an inaccessible criterion does not isolate consequence value.
An initially unreachable requirement provides little opportunity to strengthen the emerging response.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Initial acquisition?
cards.answer: Make the starting criterion attainable and initially reinforce each occurrence of the target response when appropriate.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Quality and variation?
cards.answer: Use effective consequences of suitable magnitude and variety while considering motivating operations.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Prompts and descriptive praise?
cards.answer: Combine support for correct responding with consequences and feedback tied clearly to the response.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Transfer to natural contingencies?
cards.answer: Gradually alter delays and contrived supports as performance permits rather than remove all support abruptly.

topics.title: Definition of Negative Reinforcement
topics.summary: Negative reinforcement increases future responding through stimulus termination, reduction, postponement, or prevention. It is not another name for punishment.

concepts.definition: A response produces stimulus removal, reduction, or postponement and subsequently becomes more likely.
Identify the condition making escape valuable and the circumstances under which the response produces relief.
Both increase behavior; they differ in the stimulus-change operation, not in whether the result is beneficial or harmful.

topics.takeaway: First determine whether the response increases or decreases; only then classify the stimulus operation.

scenario.prompt: Closing a window reduces an irritating draft, and closing that window becomes more frequent when the draft occurs. Which relation is described?
options: Negative reinforcement
Positive reinforcement
Negative punishment
Extinction
scenario.explanation: The response removes an ongoing condition and increases in the relevant circumstances.
rationales: The response removes an ongoing condition and increases in the relevant circumstances.
The described operation is removal or reduction of the draft.
Punishment would require a decrease in the response.
A maintaining consequence is being obtained, not withheld.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Negative reinforcement?
cards.answer: A response produces stimulus removal, reduction, or postponement and subsequently becomes more likely.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Relevant antecedent conditions?
cards.answer: Identify the condition making escape valuable and the circumstances under which the response produces relief.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Positive versus negative reinforcement?
cards.answer: Both increase behavior; they differ in the stimulus-change operation, not in whether the result is beneficial or harmful.

topics.title: Escape and Avoidance Contingencies
topics.summary: Escape and avoidance differ in the timing of the aversive event relative to the response. Avoidance may be signaled or may occur without a discrete warning signal.

concepts.definition: A response terminates or reduces stimulation already occurring.
A response postpones or prevents stimulation that would otherwise occur.
A response in the presence of a warning signal prevents the relevant event.
A response can postpone the event without the described discrete warning-signal arrangement.

topics.takeaway: Ask whether the event has already started or is being prevented.

scenario.prompt: A person checks a deadline reminder and submits a form before a late fee is imposed; timely submission becomes more likely. Which description fits the prevention component?
options: Escape from an ongoing fee
Avoidance
Respondent habituation
Positive punishment
scenario.explanation: The response prevents a future event rather than terminating a fee already imposed.
rationales: The stated fee has not yet occurred.
The response prevents a future event rather than terminating a fee already imposed.
No repeated reflex-eliciting stimulation is described.
Submitting increases rather than decreases.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Escape?
cards.answer: A response terminates or reduces stimulation already occurring.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Avoidance?
cards.answer: A response postpones or prevents stimulation that would otherwise occur.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Discriminated avoidance?
cards.answer: A response in the presence of a warning signal prevents the relevant event.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Free-operant avoidance?
cards.answer: A response can postpone the event without the described discrete warning-signal arrangement.

topics.title: Characteristics of Negative Reinforcement
topics.summary: Identifying negative reinforcement requires specifying the conditions before and after the response. The consequence may be socially mediated or produced directly, and its effectiveness depends on the arrangement.

concepts.definition: Another person removes or postpones the relevant event following the response.
The response directly reduces the relevant stimulation without another person delivering the change.
Stimuli can acquire negative-reinforcing functions through experience, while other functions do not require a prior pairing history.
Immediacy, magnitude, reliable response dependency, and available competing consequences affect the relation.

topics.takeaway: The presence of a difficult situation alone does not prove a negative-reinforcement contingency.

scenario.prompt: A learner asks for help and an instructor immediately removes an obstacle; asking for help subsequently increases. Who mediates the negative-reinforcement consequence?
options: There is no reinforcement because help is social
The worksheet as an observer
The instructor
No person, so it is necessarily automatic
scenario.explanation: The removal follows the request through another person’s action.
rationales: Socially mediated negative reinforcement is a recognized relation.
The worksheet is not the person arranging the removal.
The removal follows the request through another person’s action.
The instructor’s action is explicitly part of the consequence.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Social negative reinforcement?
cards.answer: Another person removes or postpones the relevant event following the response.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Automatic negative reinforcement?
cards.answer: The response directly reduces the relevant stimulation without another person delivering the change.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Learning history?
cards.answer: Stimuli can acquire negative-reinforcing functions through experience, while other functions do not require a prior pairing history.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Contingency features?
cards.answer: Immediacy, magnitude, reliable response dependency, and available competing consequences affect the relation.

topics.title: Applications of Negative Reinforcement
topics.summary: Negative reinforcement may contribute to both useful skills and problem behavior. Function-based intervention can arrange an acceptable response that obtains the relevant outcome rather than rely only on suppressing its prior form.

concepts.definition: Task removal following problem behavior can select that response class.
An adaptive replacement can be strengthened by access to the same relevant form of relief.
The chapter discusses positive reinforcement as another possible component when addressing behavior maintained by negative reinforcement.
Apparent effects of correction procedures require an analysis of what actually produces escape or avoidance.

topics.takeaway: Topography alone does not tell you whether an instructional procedure functions through positive or negative reinforcement.

scenario.prompt: Assessment indicates that a learner’s shouting produces breaks. The team teaches a simple break request that obtains the same outcome. What principle guides that replacement?
options: Removing all opportunities to communicate
Making the alternative require the most effort possible
Assuming every instance of shouting has the same function
Functional equivalence of the alternative response
scenario.explanation: The new response accesses the reinforcer that previously maintained shouting.
rationales: The plan explicitly teaches communication instead.
That would not follow from making an effective competing response available.
The plan depends on this learner’s assessment.
The new response accesses the reinforcer that previously maintained shouting.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Escape-maintained behavior?
cards.answer: Task removal following problem behavior can select that response class.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Alternative responding?
cards.answer: An adaptive replacement can be strengthened by access to the same relevant form of relief.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Competing reinforcement?
cards.answer: The chapter discusses positive reinforcement as another possible component when addressing behavior maintained by negative reinforcement.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Educational interpretation?
cards.answer: Apparent effects of correction procedures require an analysis of what actually produces escape or avoidance.

topics.title: Changes in Teacher and Caregiver Responding as a Function of Negative Reinforcement
topics.summary: The behavior of teachers and caregivers is also subject to contingencies. Relief from a learner’s problem behavior can strengthen an adult response even when that response contributes to maintaining the learner’s behavior.

concepts.definition: Stopping an unpleasant interaction can negatively reinforce what the caregiver did immediately before relief.
The learner’s and adult’s behaviors can each produce consequences that maintain the interaction pattern.
Specify each person’s response and consequence separately rather than use a global label such as giving in.

topics.takeaway: Identify whose behavior is being reinforced before naming the contingency.

scenario.prompt: An adult cancels a task after loud protests; the protests stop. The adult cancels similar tasks more readily later. Which adult behavior was negatively reinforced?
options: Canceling the task
All future adult behavior indiscriminately
The learner’s task completion
The adult’s hearing ability
scenario.explanation: The cancellation was followed by relief from the protests and became more likely.
rationales: The cancellation was followed by relief from the protests and became more likely.
The specified contingency concerns cancellation in similar circumstances.
That is not the adult response described.
A sensory capacity is not the operant response under analysis.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Caregiver contingency?
cards.answer: Stopping an unpleasant interaction can negatively reinforce what the caregiver did immediately before relief.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Reciprocal relations?
cards.answer: The learner’s and adult’s behaviors can each produce consequences that maintain the interaction pattern.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Analysis of both participants?
cards.answer: Specify each person’s response and consequence separately rather than use a global label such as giving in.

topics.title: Ethical Considerations in Using Negative Reinforcement
topics.summary: The authors locate an important ethical issue in the antecedent conditions arranged to make escape or access reinforcing. An effective consequence does not justify unnecessarily severe or harmful conditions.

concepts.definition: Both deprivation-based and aversive arrangements require ethical scrutiny; producing motivation is not a sufficient justification.
Aversive conditions can evoke escape, avoidance, or other responses that compete with the intended learning.
Evaluate safety, dignity, feasibility, and outcomes rather than labeling all positive procedures good and all negative procedures bad.

topics.takeaway: The arithmetic signs in reinforcement terminology do not decide whether a procedure is ethical.

scenario.prompt: A proposal creates severe discomfort solely so that its removal can reinforce a skill. What is the central concern in this section?
options: Positive reinforcement is automatically ethical in every arrangement
The severity and ethical acceptability of the antecedent arrangement
Negative reinforcement cannot increase behavior
Only the label of the consequence matters
scenario.explanation: The ability of removal to reinforce behavior does not justify an unnecessarily noxious condition.
rationales: The chapter also examines deprivation and restriction in positive-reinforcement arrangements.
The ability of removal to reinforce behavior does not justify an unnecessarily noxious condition.
It is defined by an increase.
The actual conditions and effects matter.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Severity of the establishing condition?
cards.answer: Both deprivation-based and aversive arrangements require ethical scrutiny; producing motivation is not a sufficient justification.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Competing and unwanted effects?
cards.answer: Aversive conditions can evoke escape, avoidance, or other responses that compete with the intended learning.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Intervention judgment?
cards.answer: Evaluate safety, dignity, feasibility, and outcomes rather than labeling all positive procedures good and all negative procedures bad.

topics.title: Intermittent Reinforcement
topics.summary: Reinforcement schedules specify which response occurrences produce reinforcement. Continuous reinforcement and extinction form the boundaries, with intermittent schedules reinforcing selected occurrences between them.

concepts.definition: Each occurrence of the specified response contacts reinforcement; commonly useful during initial acquisition.
Only some occurrences produce reinforcement, often useful for maintaining established behavior.
The previously maintained response no longer produces the reinforcing consequence.

topics.takeaway: Intermittent does not mean random or unsystematic; a schedule still specifies the contingency.

scenario.prompt: A new response is reinforced every time it occurs, then later only some occurrences are reinforced. Which transition is described?
options: A transition from operant to respondent behavior
Extinction to punishment
Continuous to intermittent reinforcement
Removal of all contingencies
scenario.explanation: The proportion of response occurrences producing reinforcement changes from every occurrence to selected occurrences.
rationales: Changing a reinforcement schedule does not create that distinction.
The consequence still reinforces selected responses.
The proportion of response occurrences producing reinforcement changes from every occurrence to selected occurrences.
An intermittent schedule is still a contingency.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Continuous reinforcement?
cards.answer: Each occurrence of the specified response contacts reinforcement; commonly useful during initial acquisition.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Intermittent reinforcement?
cards.answer: Only some occurrences produce reinforcement, often useful for maintaining established behavior.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Extinction boundary?
cards.answer: The previously maintained response no longer produces the reinforcing consequence.

topics.title: Defining Basic Intermittent Schedules of Reinforcement
topics.summary: Basic schedules differ along two distinctions: number of responses versus elapsed time, and fixed versus variable requirements. Interval schedules still require a response after the interval.

concepts.definition: Reinforcement follows a fixed or varying number of responses; the variable-ratio value describes an average requirement.
The first response after a fixed or varying interval can produce reinforcement.
Time elapsing is not itself sufficient on an interval schedule; a qualifying response must occur afterward.

topics.takeaway: An interval schedule is not the same as a response-independent time schedule.

scenario.prompt: The first button press after each two-minute interval produces a point. Which schedule is described?
options: Variable interval
Fixed time
Fixed ratio
Fixed interval
scenario.explanation: A response is reinforced after a fixed amount of time has elapsed.
rationales: The interval in the description is constant.
Fixed-time delivery does not depend on a button press.
The criterion is elapsed time, not a fixed response count.
A response is reinforced after a fixed amount of time has elapsed.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Fixed ratio and variable ratio?
cards.answer: Reinforcement follows a fixed or varying number of responses; the variable-ratio value describes an average requirement.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Fixed interval and variable interval?
cards.answer: The first response after a fixed or varying interval can produce reinforcement.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Response requirement?
cards.answer: Time elapsing is not itself sufficient on an interval schedule; a qualifying response must occur afterward.

topics.title: Schedule Effects and Consistency of Performance
topics.summary: Basic research reveals characteristic schedule patterns, while the chapter cautions against treating those patterns as guarantees in every applied context.

concepts.definition: Often produces a postreinforcement pause followed by rapid responding to complete the ratio.
Often produces relatively steady responding with fewer predictable postreinforcement pauses.
Often produces a pause followed by accelerating responding as the interval progresses, sometimes described as scalloping.
Often produces a relatively stable low-to-moderate response rate.
After an interval has elapsed, reinforcement remains available only for a specified additional period.

topics.takeaway: Recognize the usual pattern, but verify the observed performance instead of assuming it.

scenario.prompt: A learner repeatedly pauses after reinforcement and then responds more rapidly as a fixed time interval nears its end. Which textbook pattern does this resemble?
options: Fixed-interval scalloping
A pattern guaranteed in all applied situations
A defining property of every variable-ratio schedule
Proof that no response is required
scenario.explanation: The pause and later acceleration resemble the described FI pattern.
rationales: The pause and later acceleration resemble the described FI pattern.
The chapter warns against that generalization.
The described timing pattern is associated with FI, not VR.
An FI contingency still requires a response.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by FR pattern?
cards.answer: Often produces a postreinforcement pause followed by rapid responding to complete the ratio.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by VR pattern?
cards.answer: Often produces relatively steady responding with fewer predictable postreinforcement pauses.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by FI pattern?
cards.answer: Often produces a pause followed by accelerating responding as the interval progresses, sometimes described as scalloping.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by VI pattern?
cards.answer: Often produces a relatively stable low-to-moderate response rate.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Limited hold?
cards.answer: After an interval has elapsed, reinforcement remains available only for a specified additional period.

topics.title: Thinning Intermittent Reinforcement
topics.summary: Thinning changes a dense schedule toward a less frequent reinforcement arrangement. The transition should follow performance, using manageable increments rather than abrupt increases in requirements.

concepts.definition: Increase a response requirement or interval gradually as the behavior is maintained.
Disruption in responding can follow an abrupt or excessive increase in ratio requirements.
Clear descriptions of the contingency may assist transition; data determine whether a step is too large.

topics.takeaway: A final feasible schedule is a destination, not a reason to skip the transition.

scenario.prompt: A program jumps from reinforcement after every response to every fiftieth response, and responding collapses. Which concern is most consistent with the chapter?
options: Respondent extinction
Ratio strain
A required effect of every small schedule change
Proof the response was never learned
scenario.explanation: A sudden large increase in the response requirement can disrupt established responding.
rationales: The example concerns an operant reinforcement schedule.
A sudden large increase in the response requirement can disrupt established responding.
The problem is not an inevitable consequence of any gradual change.
The disruption follows a major contingency change.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Schedule thinning?
cards.answer: Increase a response requirement or interval gradually as the behavior is maintained.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Ratio strain?
cards.answer: Disruption in responding can follow an abrupt or excessive increase in ratio requirements.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Instructions and monitoring?
cards.answer: Clear descriptions of the contingency may assist transition; data determine whether a step is too large.

topics.title: Variations on Basic Intermittent Schedules of Reinforcement
topics.summary: Variations on basic schedules can arrange higher or lower response rates, progressively increasing work, or response variability. Select the rule that matches the performance objective.

concepts.definition: Reinforcement depends on responding above or below a rate criterion, respectively.
A rate limit decreases across intervals or stages based on performance.
Reinforcement depends on the response differing in a specified way from one or more preceding responses.
The response requirement increases within a session, allowing examination of performance as the cost rises.

topics.takeaway: A contingency for doing something differently is not the same as a contingency for doing it more often.

scenario.prompt: A game awards a point only when the learner’s answer differs from each of the previous two answers. What is the key schedule feature?
options: An interval requirement
A requirement for no responding
A lag requirement
Only a high response rate
scenario.explanation: The consequence depends on variation relative to preceding responses.
rationales: No elapsed-time criterion is specified.
The learner must respond in a different way.
The consequence depends on variation relative to preceding responses.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by DRH and DRL?
cards.answer: Reinforcement depends on responding above or below a rate criterion, respectively.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Diminishing rates?
cards.answer: A rate limit decreases across intervals or stages based on performance.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Lag schedule?
cards.answer: Reinforcement depends on the response differing in a specified way from one or more preceding responses.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Progressive ratio?

topics.title: Compound Schedules of Reinforcement
topics.summary: Compound schedules combine basic schedules. The important distinctions include simultaneous versus successive availability, signals for the components, and whether one or all requirements must be completed.

concepts.definition: Two or more independently operating contingencies are available simultaneously for different responses; allocation can be examined in relation to reinforcement.
Both arrange successive components; multiple schedules signal components with different stimuli, while mixed schedules omit those component signals.
A sequence of requirements leads to terminal reinforcement; chained schedules signal components, while tandem schedules do not.
An alternative arrangement reinforces completion of either requirement; a conjunctive arrangement requires completion of all specified requirements.
Changing reinforcement in one multiple-schedule component can be accompanied by an opposite-direction change in another unchanged component.

topics.takeaway: Use a component diagram: simultaneous or sequential, signaled or unsignaled, any requirement or all.

scenario.prompt: Two schedules alternate in sequence, and a different colored light identifies each active component. Each component can produce its own reinforcement. Which label best fits?
options: Concurrent schedule
Mixed schedule
Tandem schedule
Multiple schedule
scenario.explanation: Successive independently reinforced components are signaled by distinct stimuli.
rationales: Concurrent components are available at the same time, not only successively.
Mixed schedules do not provide those distinct component signals.

topics.title: Perspectives on Using Schedules of Reinforcement in Applied Settings
topics.summary: The authors distinguish established laboratory findings from their application in complex natural settings. They also discuss adjunctive behavior as a possible collateral product of periodic reinforcement arrangements.

concepts.definition: Schedule effects identified under controlled conditions should be checked in the actual applied arrangement.
Time-filling or collateral activity can occur in relation to periodic reinforcement for another behavior.
Directly targeting a collateral response without examining the schedule-related conditions may miss relevant variables.

topics.takeaway: A familiar schedule label is not a complete analysis of everything occurring around it.

Assume all schedules have identical effects

topics.title: Definition and Characteristics of Punishment
topics.summary: Punishment is a demonstrated reduction in future behavior following a consequence. Positive punishment adds stimulation; negative punishment removes it. These technical meanings do not establish that a procedure is appropriate.

concepts.definition: The consequence decreases future occurrences of the response class; intention or immediate interruption is not enough.
Positive punishment presents or increases a stimulus; negative punishment withdraws or decreases a stimulus.
The categories distinguish prior learning requirements and breadth of pairing histories.
A stimulus condition can occasion lower responding because that response has been punished in its presence.
Suppression may not persist when punishment is removed, particularly when reinforcement for the target remains available.

topics.takeaway: Naming a consequence a punishment requires evidence about future responding, not merely observing an immediate reaction.

scenario.prompt: A reprimand briefly interrupts a response, but the response occurs just as often in later comparable situations. What is not yet established?
options: That a stimulus was presented
A punishing function
That all reprimands reinforce behavior
That the response occurred
scenario.explanation: An interruption without a demonstrated decrease in future responding does not establish punishment.
rationales: The reprimand was a stimulus presentation.

topics.title: Factors That Influence the Effectiveness of Punishment
topics.summary: The chapter reviews variables affecting punishment, including timing, consistency, intensity, and competing reinforcement. These are functional variables to analyze, not a license to apply intrusive procedures without safeguards.

topics.title: Positive Punishment Interventions
topics.summary: The chapter describes several historically used positive-punishment procedures and distinguishes them by their operations. Recognizing those descriptions for study is separate from authorizing their use.

topics.title: Behavior Chaining Methods
topics.summary: Forward, backward, and total-task approaches differ in the order and amount of training provided. The learner’s performance and task features determine which arrangement is suitable.

scenario.prompt: An instructor completes all but the final step; the learner completes that final step and contacts the task’s outcome. Earlier steps are then added to the learner’s portion. Which procedure is described?

Backward chaining

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Backward chaining?

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Backward chaining with leap aheads?
cards.answer: Probe and bypass direct training for steps already performed adequately.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Terminal-reinforcer contact?
cards.answer: Backward chaining allows the learner to contact the terminal consequence during each instructional trial.

topics.title: Choosing a Chaining Method
topics.summary: No single chaining method is presented as universally superior. Assessment, evidence, learner abilities, task characteristics, and practical conditions guide the selection.

concepts.definition: Use component mastery and performance data rather than choose only from habit.

topics.title: Disrupting and Breaking Behavior Chains
topics.summary: Chains can be disrupted by changing links, stimuli, timing, or consequences. The chapter describes several mechanisms; choosing an approach requires understanding how the chain currently functions.

topics.title: Troubleshooting Chains
topics.summary: Troubleshooting compares the trained sequence with actual performance conditions. Similar-looking cues, missing relevant stimuli, or new competing stimuli can explain a chain that fails outside training.

topics.title: Factors Affecting the Performance of Behavior Chains
topics.summary: Chain performance depends on a complete task analysis, complexity, reinforcement arrangements, and the range of stimulus and response variations. Efficient execution and generality require attention beyond initial acquisition.

topics.title: Extinction Defined
topics.summary: Extinction names a procedure, a behavioral process, and a principle. It is not a synonym for any behavior decrease, forgetting, ignoring, or physically stopping a response.

topics.title: Extinction Procedures
topics.summary: Extinction arrangements depend on behavioral function. Withholding attention, preventing response-produced escape, or altering response-produced sensory consequences are not interchangeable procedures.

topics.summary: Extinction can be accompanied by temporary increases, new forms of responding, emotional effects, spontaneous recovery, or resurgence. These are possible patterns to anticipate and evaluate, not inevitable outcomes.

topics.title: Variables Affecting Resistance to Extinction
topics.summary: Resistance to extinction is relative persistence of responding after reinforcement stops. Reinforcement history, schedule features, current motivation, effort, and other variables can affect it.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Ethics training?
cards.answer: Use initial and continuing instruction, including discussion of actual dilemmas and practice responding to them.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Assistance-seeking supports?
cards.answer: Make consultation available and respond constructively when staff identify ambiguous or concerning situations.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Organizational contingencies?
cards.answer: Evaluate whether policies and informal consequences support ethical conduct or discourage reporting concerns.

cards.question: In this section, what is meant by Continuing review?
cards.answer: Use recurrent problems as information for improving training and systems rather than treating ethics as a one-time orientation.

topics.title: Glossary · terms and definitions
topics.summary: Search the textbook glossary, jump to its printed page, or practice its extracted definitions as flashcards. These entries preserve the book’s terminology; they are distinct from the authored chapter lessons.
topics.takeaway: Glossary definitions provide a starting point. Use the chapter discussion and source pages for conditions, exceptions, examples, and historical context.

cards.question: According to the textbook glossary, what is A-B design?
cards.answer: A two-phase experimental design consisting of a pretreatment baseline condition (A) followed by a treatment condition (B).

cards.question: According to the textbook glossary, what is A-B-A design?
cards.answer: A three-phase experimental design consisting of an initial baseline phase (A) until steady state responding (or counter-therapeutic trend) is obtained, an intervention phase in which the treatment condition (B) is implemented until the behavior has changed and steady state responding is obtained, and a return to baseline conditions (A) by withdrawing the independent variable to see whether responding "reverses" to levels observed in the initial baseline phase. (See also

cards.question: According to the textbook glossary, what is A-B-A-B design?
